html:
O'odham Jeweḍ, "the land of the O'odham", is the wide desert homeland of the O'odham peoples in southern Arizona and northern Sonora. The O'odham speak a Uto-Aztecan language and include the Tohono O'odham, the "desert people", and the Akimel O'odham, the "river people", once called Pima.

Many archaeologists link them to the Hohokam, who dug long irrigation canals in the Salt and Gila valleys. River O'odham farmed with irrigation; desert O'odham moved between summer field camps and winter wells, and gathered saguaro fruit. The Jesuit missionary Eusebio Kino worked among them from 1687 and founded missions such as San Xavier del Bac. In 1853 the Gadsden Purchase drew the border between the United States and Mexico through their land, splitting it in two.
